ripheral smear. PCR has the highest sensitivity and specificity with a rapid turnaround time, which makes it the most frequently used method of confirming anaplasmosis. Blood must be obtained before treatment or within 48 hours of antibiotic therapy. Detection of morulae by peripheral smear is seen in 25% to 75% of infected patients who have not begun treatment (Figure 1). Peripheral smear sensitivity is highest during the first week of infection.24 In the unfortunate event that a patient fatally succumbs to anaplasmosis, immunohistochemistry can be helpful with tissue obtained during autopsy.

findings.label: Interstitial pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiograph
findings.evidence: Axial image showing bilateral central and peripheral ground-glass opacities (black arrows).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial chest CT from a case report of human granulocytic anaplasmosis shows bilateral ground-glass opacities; findings are nonspecific and were interpreted as COVID-19-like pneumonia, so attribution is supported by the disease-focused article context but remains atypical. B: Coronal chest CT from a human granulocytic anaplasmosis case report shows bilateral ground-glass opacities; the pattern is nonspecific and mimics COVID-19 pneumonia, making the manifestation atypical for anaplasmosis.
panels.attribution_text: Stice et al. Anchoring on COVID-19: A Case Report of Human Granulocytic Anaplasmosis Masquerading as COVID-19.. Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine 2021. doi:10.5811/cpcem.2021.4.51970. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure Image.
panels.figure_caption: Computed tomography angiography of the chest. Black arrows indicate ground glass opacities. (A) Axial image showing bilateral central and peripheral ground-glass opacities. (B) Coronal image demonstrating bilateral ground-glass opacities in upper and lower lung fields.
in_text_mentions: ia. Blood cultures were drawn, and the patient was started on cefepime and vancomycin in the event his presentation was a result of a bacterial pneumonia. A computed tomography (CT) angiography of the chest was obtained due to the elevated D-dimer and respiratory distress. No pulmonary embolism was present, but the CT did reveal extensive bilateral infiltrates consistent with a COVID-19 pneumonia (Image). After results had been obtained, a report from the transferring ED contained similar lab results, including a negative COVID-19 PCR. The patient was then admitted to the ICU for ongoing care.
